title: Real Analysis II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Real Analysis II curriculum, building on MTH207 (introductory real analysis): sequences and series of functions, pointwise versus uniform convergence, the Weierstrass M-test, Riemann integration and its properties, the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, improper integrals, an introduction to functions of several variables, and an introduction to metric spaces (open/closed sets, compactness, connectedness).

questions.question: A sequence of functions fn converges pointwise to f on a set S if:
options: for each x in S, fn(x) → f(x) as n → ∞
questions.correct_answer: for each x in S, fn(x) → f(x) as n → ∞
questions.explanation: Pointwise convergence only requires convergence of fn(x) to f(x) at each individual point, with the rate of convergence possibly varying by point.

questions.question: A sequence of functions fn converges uniformly to f on S if:
options: for every ε>0, there exists N such that |fn(x)-f(x)|<ε for all x in S and all n≥N
fn(x)→f(x) for each x separately with no common N
questions.correct_answer: for every ε>0, there exists N such that |fn(x)-f(x)|<ε for all x in S and all n≥N
questions.explanation: Uniform convergence strengthens pointwise convergence by requiring a single N that works simultaneously for every point in S.

questions.question: The sequence fn(x) = x^n on [0,1] converges pointwise to:
options: f(x) = 0 for x in [0,1), and f(1) = 1
f(x) = 0 for all x including x=1
questions.correct_answer: f(x) = 0 for x in [0,1), and f(1) = 1
questions.explanation: For 0 ≤ x < 1, x^n → 0, while at x=1, x^n = 1 for all n, giving this discontinuous pointwise limit.

questions.question: The sequence fn(x) = x^n on [0,1] illustrates that:
options: the pointwise limit of continuous functions need not be continuous, so the convergence is not uniform
pointwise and uniform convergence are always equivalent
questions.correct_answer: the pointwise limit of continuous functions need not be continuous, so the convergence is not uniform
questions.explanation: Since each x^n is continuous but the pointwise limit is discontinuous at x=1, the convergence cannot be uniform on [0,1] (uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous).

questions.question: If fn → f uniformly on [a,b] and each fn is continuous, then:
questions.correct_answer: f is continuous on [a,b]
questions.explanation: Uniform convergence preserves continuity: the uniform limit of a sequence of continuous functions is itself continuous.

questions.question: If fn → f uniformly on [a,b] and each fn is Riemann integrable, then:
questions.correct_answer: ∫a^b fn dx → ∫a^b f dx
questions.explanation: Uniform convergence justifies interchanging the limit and integral: the limit of the integrals equals the integral of the limit.

questions.question: The Weierstrass M-test is used to establish:
options: uniform convergence of a series of functions
questions.correct_answer: uniform convergence of a series of functions
questions.explanation: The M-test states that if |fn(x)| ≤ Mn for all x in S with ΣMn convergent, then Σfn converges uniformly (and absolutely) on S.

questions.question: By the Weierstrass M-test, the series Σ sin(nx)/n^2 converges uniformly on the real line because:
options: the series is a power series
questions.correct_answer: |sin(nx)/n^2| ≤ 1/n^2 and Σ1/n^2 converges
questions.explanation: Since |sin(nx)| ≤ 1 for all x, the terms are dominated by the convergent p-series Σ1/n^2, satisfying the M-test hypothesis.

questions.question: For a bounded function f on [a,b], the Riemann upper sum U(f,P) with respect to a partition P is defined using:
options: the supremum of f on each subinterval
the infimum of f on each subinterval
the value of f at the left endpoint only
questions.correct_answer: the supremum of f on each subinterval
questions.explanation: The upper Riemann sum uses Mi = sup{f(x): x in the i-th subinterval} multiplied by the subinterval width, summed over all subintervals.

questions.question: A bounded function f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] if and only if:
options: for every ε>0, there exists a partition P such that U(f,P) - L(f,P) < ε
questions.correct_answer: for every ε>0, there exists a partition P such that U(f,P) - L(f,P) < ε
questions.explanation: This is the Riemann integrability criterion: the upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close by refining the partition.

questions.question: Which of these functions is Riemann integrable on [0,1]?
options: the Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals)
questions.correct_answer: a continuous function on [0,1]
questions.explanation: Every continuous function on a closed bounded interval is Riemann integrable; the Dirichlet function is a classic example of a bounded function that is NOT Riemann integrable.

questions.question: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Riemann integral version) states that if f is continuous on [a,b] and F(x) = ∫a^x f(t)dt, then:
options: F is differentiable and F'(x) = f(x)
questions.correct_answer: F is differentiable and F'(x) = f(x)
questions.explanation: This is the first part of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, linking differentiation and integration for continuous functions.

questions.question: The Riemann-Stieltjes integral ∫a^b f dα generalizes the Riemann integral by:
options: using an increasing (or bounded variation) function α(x) instead of x itself as the integrator
removing the need for a partition
questions.correct_answer: using an increasing (or bounded variation) function α(x) instead of x itself as the integrator
questions.explanation: The Riemann-Stieltjes integral replaces the increments Δx with Δα = α(xi) - α(xi-1), generalizing the ordinary Riemann integral (recovered when α(x)=x).

questions.question: If α(x) is a step function with a jump of size c at point x0, then for continuous f, the Riemann-Stieltjes integral ∫f dα picks out:
options: the integral of f over the whole interval
questions.correct_answer: c·f(x0)
questions.explanation: A jump discontinuity in the integrator α of size c contributes exactly c·f(x0) to the Riemann-Stieltjes integral, at the point of the jump.

questions.question: An improper integral of the first kind is one where:
options: the interval of integration is unbounded (e.g. extends to ∞)
the integrand has a removable discontinuity
the interval is finite and the integrand is bounded
questions.correct_answer: the interval of integration is unbounded (e.g. extends to ∞)
questions.explanation: Improper integrals of the first kind involve infinite limits of integration, evaluated as a limit of proper integrals over finite intervals.

questions.question: The improper integral ∫1^∞ (1/x^p) dx converges if and only if:
questions.explanation: This is the standard p-integral test: ∫1^∞ x^{-p}dx converges exactly when p > 1 and diverges otherwise.

questions.question: An improper integral of the second kind arises when:
options: the integrand is unbounded near a point in the interval of integration
questions.correct_answer: the integrand is unbounded near a point in the interval of integration
questions.explanation: This type occurs when f(x) becomes infinite at or near an endpoint (or interior point) of a finite interval, requiring a limiting definition.

questions.question: For a function f(x,y) of two variables, the partial derivative ∂f/∂x is computed by:
options: differentiating with respect to x while treating y as constant
differentiating with respect to both x and y simultaneously
questions.correct_answer: differentiating with respect to x while treating y as constant
questions.explanation: A partial derivative measures the rate of change with respect to one variable while holding all other variables fixed.

questions.question: A function f(x,y) is differentiable at a point if:
options: it can be well-approximated by a linear (affine) function near that point
questions.correct_answer: it can be well-approximated by a linear (affine) function near that point
questions.explanation: Differentiability of a multivariable function requires the existence of a linear approximation (total derivative) whose error vanishes faster than the distance to the point, which is stronger than merely having partial derivatives.

questions.question: Clairaut's (Schwarz's) Theorem on mixed partial derivatives states that if fxy and fyx are both continuous, then:
questions.correct_answer: fxy = fyx
questions.explanation: When the mixed second partial derivatives are continuous, the order of differentiation does not matter, so fxy = fyx.

questions.question: A metric space (X,d) consists of a set X together with a function d satisfying:
options: non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, and the triangle inequality
questions.correct_answer: non-negativity, identity of indiscernibles, symmetry, and the triangle inequality
questions.explanation: These four axioms define a metric: d(x,y)≥0, d(x,y)=0 iff x=y, d(x,y)=d(y,x), and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z).

questions.question: In a metric space, an open ball B(x0, r) is defined as:
questions.correct_answer: {x ∈ X : d(x,x0) < r}
questions.explanation: An open ball of radius r centered at x0 is the set of all points strictly within distance r of x0.

questions.question: A subset U of a metric space X is called open if:
options: every point of U has an open ball around it entirely contained in U
U contains all its limit points
questions.correct_answer: every point of U has an open ball around it entirely contained in U
questions.explanation: This is the defining property of an open set in a metric space: each point is an interior point.

questions.question: A subset F of a metric space is called closed if:
questions.correct_answer: its complement is open
questions.explanation: By definition, a closed set is one whose complement in the space is open; equivalently, it contains all of its limit points.

questions.question: A metric space X is called compact if:
options: every open cover of X has a finite subcover
questions.correct_answer: every open cover of X has a finite subcover
questions.explanation: This is the general topological definition of compactness, which for metric spaces is equivalent to sequential compactness.

questions.question: The Heine-Borel Theorem states that a subset of R^n (with the usual metric) is compact if and only if it is:
questions.correct_answer: closed and bounded
questions.explanation: In Euclidean space, Heine-Borel gives the concrete characterization: compact sets are exactly those that are both closed and bounded.

questions.question: A continuous image of a compact set (under a continuous function) is always:
questions.correct_answer: compact
questions.explanation: Continuous functions preserve compactness: if f is continuous and K is compact, then f(K) is compact.

questions.question: A metric space X is called connected if:
options: it cannot be partitioned into two nonempty disjoint open sets
questions.correct_answer: it cannot be partitioned into two nonempty disjoint open sets
questions.explanation: Connectedness means X has no separation into two nonempty disjoint open subsets whose union is X.

questions.question: A function f: X → Y between metric spaces is continuous at x0 if:
options: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that d(x,x0)<δ implies d(f(x),f(x0))<ε
questions.correct_answer: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that d(x,x0)<δ implies d(f(x),f(x0))<ε
questions.explanation: This is the standard epsilon-delta definition of continuity generalized to metric spaces using the two spaces' respective metrics.

questions.question: The interval [0,1] with the usual metric on R is an example of a set that is:
questions.correct_answer: both compact and connected
questions.explanation: [0,1] is closed and bounded (hence compact by Heine-Borel) and is an interval, hence connected.
